clue.text: A champion engine-driver or two

parts.note: BR stands for British Railways, so an engine-driver of the 1950s was a BR man
an ace is a champion, the best at something

explanation.surface: A clue praising a top-class train driver, or perhaps a pair of them.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'A champion engine-driver' as 'a BR ace': BR (British Railways, the UK's nationalised railway) comes first, then ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace is a pair, as in a brace of pheasants.

clue.text: Row over cow perhaps ?

parts.note: a fight over a bovine, read as a quarrel about cattle but meaning a Spanish arena contest

explanation.surface: Neighbours quarrelling about a farm animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The bull (the male of the cow's kind) sits over the fight in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish arena spectacle where a matador fights with cattle.

clue.text: Religious head of Scottish home

indicators.note: head of means only the front part of the house's name is used

parts.note: Abbotsford was Sir Walter Scott's home in the Borders

explanation.surface: The minister in charge of a Scottish household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Religious' is a noun here: a member of a monastic order. 'Religious head' is the false reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A monk heading an abbey is a member of a religious order, which is what a religious is.

clue.text: Porsena for instance discomfiting centaurs

indicators.note: discomfiting means throwing into confusion, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: An ancient warrior king routing a herd of mythical horsemen.
explanation.walkthrough: Lars Porsena of Clusium, from Macaulay's Horatius, was an Etruscan king.
explanation.definitionFit: Porsena was a king from Etruria, the ancient Italian land north of Rome.

clue.text: Terrier gets medal round Gold Mountain

parts.note: a cairn is a small Scottish breed of terrier

indicators.note: the medal's letters go round the outside of the gold's letters

parts.note: GM is the George Medal, a British gallantry award
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A dog wins a medal at a show, with gold mentioned somewhere nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts GM around OR to give GORM, which follows CAIRN.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cairngorms are a Scottish range, and Cairn Gorm is one peak in it.

clue.text: Two proverbially in order for an explorer

definitions.text: Two proverbially in order for an explorer

parts.words: Two proverbially in order for an explorer
parts.note: the proverb says too many in the kitchen spoil the broth; two, sounding like too, points to that proverb, and Captain James is the explorer

explanation.surface: Two people arranged, as the saying goes, to go exploring.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain James Cook charted the Pacific; the proverb 'too many cooks spoil the broth' supplies the 'Two'.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain James of that name was the British navigator who charted much of the Pacific.

clue.text: Establishes the work was Justinian's

definitions.meaning: a legal textbook compiled under Emperor Justinian

explanation.definitionFit: To institute is to found; Justinian's Institutes was a Roman law handbook.

clue.text: They form the heart of the matter

definitions.text: They form the heart of the matter

parts.words: They form the heart of the matter
parts.note: read literally: the dense central parts of atoms, which make up matter

explanation.surface: A phrase about the essence of an issue.
explanation.definitionFit: Atomic cores sit at the centre of every atom, so they lie at the heart of physical matter.

clue.text: Use periscope to see what children do to an old woman's shoe ?

definitions.meaning: look over a crowd, as a spectator does with a cardboard periscope

definitions.text: what children do to an old woman's shoe ?
definitions.meaning: the nursery-rhyme old woman lived in a shoe and had so many children she didn't know what to do

explanation.definitionFit: To pack too many in, as the rhyme's children packed the shoe; split, it is seeing over a throng.

clue.text: Came across, about to return choral work

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the word met is wrapped round the other piece

parts.note: met means came across, encountered

indicators.note: return tells us the little word goes back on itself

explanation.surface: Someone happened upon a choir piece and is about to go back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' reverses TO to OT; 'about' puts MET around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a short unaccompanied sacred choral composition.

clue.text: Fame spurs one to live these days, said Milton

definitions.text: Fame spurs one to live these days, said Milton

parts.words: Fame spurs one to live these days, said Milton
parts.note: a paraphrase of Milton's Lycidas, where fame is the spur to scorn delights and live days of hard toil

explanation.surface: A literary quotation about ambition, credited to the poet Milton.
explanation.walkthrough: Lycidas reads 'Fame is the spur ... To scorn delights, and live laborious days'; the missing adjective is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Days of hard, toilsome effort are the ones Milton says fame drives a person to live.

clue.text: Many went away and split

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword stand-in for many
left means departed or went away

explanation.surface: A crowd departed and broke up.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleft is a past participle meaning cut or divided in two.

clue.text: Thief's unusual object of worship

indicators.note: unusual tells us the letters of the word are set out in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A burglar has a strange devotion to some idol.
explanation.definitionFit: A fetish is an object revered for supposed magical power, an idol or charm.

clue.text: A patient for one kind of surgeon in two hundred at last?

definitions.text: A patient for one kind of surgeon in two hundred at last?

indicators.note: last says the word at is placed at the end
one and the surgeon go inside the two hundred, set between its letters

parts.note: C is a hundred in Roman numerals, so two hundred is two Cs
I is the Roman numeral one
a vet is a veterinary surgeon

explanation.surface: Among two hundred animals, one finally gets to see the animal doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts IVET inside CC (CIVETC); 'last' puts AT at the end. The whole clue describes the answer: an animal brought to a vet.
explanation.definitionFit: A civet is a catlike carnivore, the sort of animal a veterinary surgeon might treat.

clue.text: Cigarette for instance-best seller in camp ?

definitions.meaning: Cigarette is the camp-follower heroine of Ouida's novel Under Two Flags
a woman who sold food and drink to soldiers in the field

explanation.definitionFit: A canteen-woman following French regiments, as Ouida's Cigarette does.

clue.text: Like similarly plumaged birds

parts.note: alludes to the proverb that birds of a feather flock together, so such birds keep company

explanation.surface: A description of birds with matching feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: Gregarious means fond of company, living in flocks, as birds of a feather do in the proverb.

clue.text: What a ducky quilt !

parts.note: ducky reads as sweet or lovely but means made from ducks, filled with their soft feathers

explanation.surface: An admiring cry at a pretty bedcover.
explanation.definitionFit: A quilt stuffed with the soft breast feathers of a sea duck.

clue.text: Sound of waves breaking at the harbour bar ?

definitions.meaning: a deep roar or resonant noise, like surf on rocks
a barrier of chained logs or a net stretched across a harbour mouth

explanation.definitionFit: Boom is both a deep resonant noise and a floating barrier closing a harbour.

clue.text: Dodgsonian type of clue for " threat "

parts.note: the clue's word threat is what you get if the letters of a hat-maker's trade name are jumbled, mad being the anagram signal

explanation.surface: A remark about how Lewis Carroll would clue a word meaning menace.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Dodgson wrote as Lewis Carroll; the character's name read as an anagram clue says 'HATTER, mad', which yields 'threat'.
explanation.definitionFit: The tea-party host in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is one of Carroll's creations.

clue.text: Something going down the line

parts.note: the line is a family line of descent, not a railway

explanation.surface: Something travelling along a railway track.
explanation.definitionFit: A treasured family possession passed from one generation to the next.

clue.text: It's bound, we hear, to turn twice a day

indicators.note: we hear tells us a word is said aloud and a like-sounding one is meant

parts.note: bound means tied up

explanation.surface: Something that is obliged, apparently, to change direction every twelve hours.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea's rise and fall reverses roughly twice daily.

clue.text: Uncapped having only Pooh's mental ability, say?

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is spoken aloud and a like-sounding word is meant

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh calls himself a bear of very little brain, so this means having a bear's head

explanation.surface: A player without international honours who has the brains of a toy bear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncapped' suggests a sportsman with no caps (international appearances); here it just means hatless.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncapped means without a hat, with the head uncovered.

clue.text: The main trouble with America is bad blood

indicators.note: trouble works as a verb, disturbing the letters into a new order

parts.note: US is the United States

explanation.surface: A remark that the chief problem with the USA is enmity.
explanation.definitionFit: Animus means hostility or ill feeling.

clue.text: Numbers wooing a lady-love

parts.note: numbers are songs or pieces of music, here sung to court a sweetheart

explanation.surface: Lots of suitors chasing one woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' looks like a crowd of suitors; it means musical numbers, songs.
explanation.definitionFit: Songs sung at night beneath a beloved's window are the classic courting music.

clue.text: He makes S Subscribes to symbols

definitions.meaning: writes a name at the foot of, as with a signature
marks standing for something, like plus and minus

explanation.definitionFit: Signs means writes one's name on, and also marks used as tokens.

clue.text: A jolly girl in the fleet

parts.note: a jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine, RM
Ada is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A cheerful young woman at sea with the navy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish Armada of 1588 was a great fleet of warships.

clue.text: A boy raised as a non-native

indicators.note: raised in a down entry means the word is written upwards, so reversed

parts.note: Neil is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A lad brought up as a foreigner.
explanation.definitionFit: An alien is a foreigner, someone not native to the country.

clue.text: Measure cuckoo takes to wake robin ?

definitions.meaning: a measure of liquid, half a quart
cuckoo plus this word makes the wild arum's name, also called wake robin

explanation.definitionFit: A pint is a unit of measure; added to cuckoo it names the plant wake robin.

clue.text: Note Othello returning with a bride

parts.note: G is a musical note

indicators.note: returning means the word goes back the way it came, read right to left

parts.note: Othello is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice

explanation.surface: A message saying Shakespeare's hero is back home with his new wife.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridegroom is the man accompanied by a bride at a wedding.

clue.text: He makes short work of Brown in tricky two-step

indicators.note: the name goes inside the rearranged letters
tricky suggests the letters are juggled into a new order

parts.note: II is two in Roman numerals
taken as written
Tom Brown is the hero of Tom Brown's Schooldays

explanation.surface: Someone quickly beats a man called Brown at a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tricky' rearranges II and STEP to EPIIST; 'in' places TOM inside it. 'Two-step' looks like the dance but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: One who writes abridgements or summaries reduces long works to short ones.

clue.text: Getting on with changing ten scenes

indicators.note: changing tells us the letters swap places to form another word

explanation.surface: A theatre production growing older as it shifts sets ten times.
explanation.definitionFit: Senescent means ageing, growing old.

clue.text: Not the army type of key

definitions.meaning: the opposite of major, an army rank
a musical key with a flattened third, as against a major key

explanation.definitionFit: Minor is the opposite of major, both the army rank's name and a kind of musical key.
